title: Nghĩ Giàu Làm Giàu (Think and Grow Rich, Vietnamese edition, Yuan Phong translation)
author: Napoleon Hill
summary:
Think and Grow Rich grew out of a twenty-year research project Napoleon Hill said he undertook at the urging of steel magnate Andrew Carnegie, who wanted someone to distill the common traits of America's wealthiest self-made men into a teachable system. Hill interviewed and studied hundreds of successful figures — among them Henry Ford, Thomas Edison, and Carnegie himself — and organized what he found into thirteen "steps" or principles that, he argued, explain why some people convert ambition into fortune while others with equal or greater talent do not. The core claim of the book is not that money follows luck or connections, but that it follows a specific, repeatable state of mind: a burning, specific desire converted into a definite plan and backed by unwavering persistence.

The book opens with the idea that "thoughts are things" — that a clearly defined desire, held with faith and translated into a written, dated plan, sets in motion behavior that eventually produces its physical equivalent. From there Hill builds outward through faith, autosuggestion (the deliberate, repeated impression of a goal on the subconscious mind), specialized knowledge (as distinct from general education), imagination, organized planning, and decision. He is emphatic that indecision and procrastination are close cousins of fear, and that the wealthy men he studied were almost uniformly fast, firm decision-makers who were slow to change their minds once a decision was made.

A second major thread concerns persistence and the "Mastermind" principle — the idea that two or more minds working in harmony toward a definite purpose generate a third, intangible force greater than the sum of the individuals involved. Hill also devotes substantial space to the transmutation of sexual energy into creative and entrepreneurial drive, a section that was considered daring for its time and remains one of the book's more debated chapters. He closes with a discussion of the subconscious mind, the brain as a broadcasting and receiving station for thought, the sixth sense, and a final chapter cataloguing the "six ghosts of fear" — the fears of poverty, criticism, ill health, loss of love, old age, and death — that he argues sabotage most people's pursuit of their definite chief aim.

Running underneath all thirteen principles is a single mechanical claim that gives the book its title: intense, specific, faith-backed desire, repeated to the subconscious mind and acted on with a definite plan, will reorganize a person's behavior and circumstances toward the object of that desire. Hill frames this as a discoverable natural law rather than motivational rhetoric, and structures the book so each chapter both stands alone as a lesson and builds toward this cumulative thesis. Nearly a century after its 1937 publication, it remains one of the best-selling personal-development books ever written and the direct ancestor of much of the modern "mindset" and goal-setting literature.

sections.title: Introduction: The Man Who "Thought" His Way into Partnership with Carnegie
sections.summary: This opening chapter sets out Hill's origin story for the book: a chance meeting with Andrew Carnegie that led to a multi-decade commission to study the psychology of achievement across hundreds of successful Americans. Hill uses the chapter to establish his central promise — that success leaves a traceable, teachable pattern — and to introduce the story of Edwin C. Barnes, a man who resolved to become Thomas Edison's business partner with no money or connections and eventually did. The chapter's substance is less instructional than scene-setting: it exists to establish Hill's authority and to plant the book's central metaphor, that thought held with sufficient intensity behaves like a physical cause with a physical effect. It hands off directly into the first formal principle, desire, by asking the reader what they would attempt if they knew failure were impossible.
keyLessons: A stated research pedigree (real interviews with real self-made figures) is the book's foundational claim to authority, distinct from its prescriptions.
The Barnes story is used to argue that resourcelessness is not disqualifying if desire is specific and decision is total.
The book positions itself as describing a law, not offering opinion — a framing worth noticing critically as well as absorbing.

sections.title: Desire: The Starting Point of All Achievement
sections.summary: This chapter lays out Hill's six-step method for turning a vague wish into what he calls a "burning desire": fix an exact amount or outcome, decide what you will give in return, set a definite date, create a definite plan, write a clear statement of all four, and read that statement aloud twice daily. He illustrates the principle with Henry Ford's refusal to abandon the V8 engine despite his engineers insisting it was impossible, framing stubborn, specific desire as the mechanism that kept Ford's team working until a solution appeared. The chapter's underlying argument is that most people fail not from lack of ability but from never converting a wish into a dated, written, specific commitment. It closes by distinguishing a wish from a desire, setting up faith — needed to sustain desire against discouragement — as the next principle.
keyLessons: Vague wanting rarely produces results; specificity (amount, date, plan) is what Hill claims converts desire into a working commitment.
Writing and reading a goal statement daily is presented as a mechanical habit, not just motivational fluff.
Persistence in the face of expert skepticism (the Ford V8 example) is framed as a feature of desire, not stubbornness for its own sake.

sections.title: Faith: Visualization of, and Belief in, Attainment of Desire
sections.summary: Here Hill argues that faith is a state of mind that can be deliberately induced through autosuggestion — repeated self-instruction — rather than something a person either has or lacks by temperament. He introduces the idea that the subconscious mind cannot distinguish between a vividly imagined experience and a real one, and that repeated, emotionally charged affirmation of a goal will eventually be acted upon by the subconscious as if it were fact. The chapter includes his often-quoted claim that "whatever the mind can conceive and believe, it can achieve," and links faith directly to self-confidence, offering a five-point self-confidence formula readers are told to memorize and repeat. It transitions into autosuggestion as the mechanical process by which that faith is actually installed.
keyLessons: Faith is treated as a trainable skill via repetition, not a fixed personality trait.
The subconscious is described as unable to separate vividly imagined belief from lived fact — the basis for the book's affirmation techniques.
A written self-confidence formula, repeated aloud, is offered as a concrete daily practice.

sections.title: Autosuggestion: The Medium for Influencing the Subconscious Mind
sections.summary: This short chapter formalizes the mechanism introduced in the previous one: the deliberate, repeated, emotionally intense communication of a goal to one's own subconscious mind. Hill insists that repetition without feeling is ineffective — the reader must work up genuine emotion while repeating their desire statement for it to register. He ties this to the earlier six-step desire formula, instructing the reader to read their written statement aloud, with feeling, immediately before sleep and immediately upon waking. The chapter closes by warning that negative, fearful thoughts are absorbed by the same channel, setting up the following chapter's emphasis on specialized knowledge as a tool for productive, rather than merely hopeful, thinking.
keyLessons: Repetition alone is not enough; Hill insists emotional intensity is what makes autosuggestion effective.
The same subconscious channel that can be directed toward goals can also absorb fear and doubt, making self-talk hygiene important.
Practicing the desire statement at the start and end of each day is presented as the discipline that makes the principle actionable.

sections.title: Specialized Knowledge: Personal Experiences or Observations
sections.summary: Hill draws a sharp distinction between general knowledge, which he considers largely useless for wealth-building on its own, and specialized knowledge, organized and directed toward a definite purpose through a plan. He argues that formal education is neither necessary nor sufficient, citing Henry Ford's famously limited schooling and his practice of surrounding himself with specialists — the germ of the Mastermind principle developed later. The chapter advises readers to identify exactly what specialized knowledge their definite purpose requires and to acquire it deliberately, whether through study, training, or partnership with others who already possess it. It leads into imagination as the faculty that shapes raw knowledge into workable plans.
keyLessons: General education is treated as separate from, and less valuable than, knowledge organized around a specific goal.
Not knowing something yourself is not a barrier if you can access it through study or through people who do know it.
Identifying the exact knowledge gap standing between you and your definite purpose is framed as a concrete planning step.

sections.title: Imagination: The Workshop of the Mind
sections.summary: This chapter presents imagination as the faculty that shapes desire and knowledge into a concrete plan, distinguishing "synthetic" imagination (recombining existing ideas) from "creative" imagination (which Hill associates with flashes of intuition). He argues that essentially all Ideas, inventions, and businesses originate as combinations of previously existing elements rearranged in a new way, and that this recombination is a skill that improves with deliberate use. The chapter includes several brief case examples of fortunes built on a single reorganized idea rather than a wholly novel invention. It hands off to organized planning as the discipline that turns an imagined idea into a sequenced, executable plan.
keyLessons: Most valuable ideas are new combinations of old elements, not creations from nothing — lowering the bar for what counts as an "original" idea worth pursuing.
Imagination, like a muscle, is presented as something that strengthens with regular, deliberate use.
An idea alone is inert; the following principle (organized planning) is what the book claims makes it actionable.

sections.title: Organized Planning: The Crystallization of Desire into Action
sections.summary: Hill lays out the practical machinery of achievement here: forming a Mastermind alliance of people whose knowledge and resources complete your own, and building a specific, written, sequenced plan of action. He gives detailed guidance on leadership versus followership, the causes of failure in leadership, and a lengthy inventory of thirty-one common causes of failure that the reader is told to use as a self-audit. The chapter's emphasis is that a plan should be treated as provisional and revised the moment it proves unworkable, rather than abandoned along with the underlying goal. It closes by insisting that persistence through inevitable plan revisions is what separates achievers from quitters, setting up the dedicated chapter on decision that follows.
keyLessons: A Mastermind group is defined narrowly: people who supply capability you lack, working in harmony toward one aim, not merely a supportive social circle.
Plans are meant to be revised repeatedly without treating revision as evidence the goal itself was wrong.
The thirty-one causes of failure are offered as a structured self-diagnostic rather than a motivational list.

sections.title: Decision: The Mastery of Procrastination
sections.summary: This chapter argues that analysis of hundreds of wealthy individuals showed a consistent habit of reaching decisions quickly and firmly, and changing them slowly if at all — the mirror image of how Hill claims most unsuccessful people behave. He treats indecision as the practical form fear takes in daily life, and procrastination as its close relative, both of which quietly erode a definite chief aim over time. The chapter includes the well-known account of the 1776 Declaration of Independence signers as an extended illustration of decisive commitment under real risk. It transitions into persistence, since Hill treats firm decision-making as the beginning of a commitment that must then be sustained.
keyLessons: Fast, firm decisions and slow, reluctant reversals are presented as a measurable habit of the successful people Hill studied.
Indecision is reframed not as caution but as fear operating under a more socially acceptable name.
A decision is treated as the start of a test of persistence, not the end of the work.

sections.title: Persistence: The Sustained Effort Necessary to Induce Faith
sections.summary: Hill calls persistence "to the character of man as carbon is to steel," and treats it as the single most commonly missing ingredient among people who otherwise have desire, knowledge, and a plan. He provides a self-analysis checklist of the symptoms of a lack of persistence and describes four simple steps to develop it: a definite purpose backed by burning desire, a definite plan, a mind closed to discouraging influences, and a friendly alliance with people who encourage the plan. The chapter frames persistence as trainable through habit rather than as an innate trait some people simply have more of. It leads into the Mastermind's "power" chapter, since Hill treats organized effort as a force multiplier for individual persistence.
keyLessons: Persistence is presented as a developed habit with identifiable symptoms of its absence, not a fixed character trait.
Hill's four-step persistence-building method centers on closing off discouraging input as much as on effort itself.
Surrounding yourself with people who reinforce rather than undermine your plan is treated as a persistence strategy, not just moral support.

sections.title: Power of the Master Mind: The Driving Force
sections.summary: This chapter formally defines the Mastermind principle as coordination of knowledge and effort between two or more people working in a spirit of harmony toward a definite purpose, producing what Hill calls a third mind more powerful than either individual's alone. He distinguishes this from ordinary cooperation by emphasizing that genuine harmony, not merely shared logistics, is what generates the effect, and gives Carnegie's steel-industry team as his primary illustration. The chapter also introduces Hill's claim about accumulating "power" as organized, directed knowledge, positioning money-making as fundamentally a power-organizing activity. It hands off to the sexual-transmutation chapter by raising emotion and energy as the fuel behind sustained organized effort.
keyLessons: A Mastermind requires genuine harmony among participants, not just coordinated activity, according to Hill's definition.
Power, in Hill's usage, means organized knowledge directed toward a definite end — not influence or authority in the ordinary sense.
Individual achievement is reframed throughout this chapter as fundamentally a group-organizing skill.

sections.title: The Mystery of Sex Transmutation
sections.summary: Hill argues that sexual energy is the most powerful of human emotions and that it can be deliberately redirected ("transmuted") into creative, entrepreneurial, and artistic drive rather than expressed only physically. He claims that a disproportionate number of history's highly achieving men reached their peak output during periods of strong romantic or sexual stimulation channeled into work, and lists ten stimulants of the mind more broadly, of which sex desire is presented as the strongest. The chapter is among the most historically debated in the book, resting on claims about historical figures that are not independently verifiable and reflecting the gender assumptions of its 1937 context. It transitions into the chapter on the subconscious mind by treating transmuted emotional energy as the "fuel" that autosuggestion and faith act upon.
keyLessons: Hill treats strong emotion generally, and sexual energy specifically, as a redirectable fuel for ambitious work rather than something to be merely managed or suppressed.
The chapter's historical claims about specific achievers are presented as evidence but are largely unverifiable and should be read as illustrative rather than proven.
The framing throughout is heteronormative and centered on male achievement, reflecting its era rather than a universal claim.

sections.title: The Subconscious Mind: The Connecting Link
sections.summary: This chapter describes the subconscious as a mediating field between conscious thought and what Hill calls "Infinite Intelligence," through which properly charged, emotionalized thought becomes translated into a real-world plan or opportunity. He reiterates that only thoughts mixed with strong emotion or feeling are acted upon by the subconscious, tying this chapter tightly back to autosuggestion and faith. The chapter offers little new practical instruction beyond restating the emotional-intensity requirement, functioning more as a bridge toward the more overtly metaphysical material that follows. It hands off directly into the chapter on the brain as a broadcasting station.
keyLessons: The subconscious mind is presented as a mechanism that only responds to emotionally charged thought, reinforcing earlier chapters rather than introducing new technique.
This chapter marks the point where the book's claims shift from psychological to more explicitly metaphysical territory.
Readers are encouraged to treat emotional intensity, not sheer repetition, as the active ingredient in all the mental-discipline chapters combined.

sections.title: The Brain: A Broadcasting and Receiving Station for Thought
sections.summary: Hill proposes, without scientific backing, that the human brain functions like a radio transmitter and receiver, capable of broadcasting emotionalized thought and picking up the emotionalized thought of others — his mechanism for phenomena like sudden inspiration or apparent telepathy between Mastermind partners. He uses this idea to explain why Mastermind alliances feel to participants like they generate ideas beyond what any individual brought to the table. The chapter is speculative even by the standards of the rest of the book and is best read as a period-appropriate metaphor for intuition and collaborative creativity rather than a literal mechanism. It leads into the sixth sense chapter, which extends the same broadcasting metaphor toward what Hill calls the "door to the temple of wisdom."
keyLessons: The broadcasting-station idea is offered as an explanatory metaphor, not an evidenced mechanism, and should be read that way.
It is used narratively to account for the felt experience of collaborative "spark" inside a well-functioning Mastermind group.
Readers looking for the book's actionable content will find little new practice here beyond the metaphor itself.

sections.title: The Sixth Sense: The Door to the Temple of Wisdom
sections.summary: In the final substantive chapter, Hill describes a sixth sense — a faculty he says develops only after mastery of the previous twelve principles — through which "Infinite Intelligence" is said to communicate ideas, warnings, and plans without conscious effort. He presents this largely through personal testimony, including an extended account of imagined meetings with historical figures he calls his "Invisible Counselors," used as a deliberate visualization exercise rather than a literal claim of spirit contact. The chapter functions as the capstone of the book's philosophical arc, positioning intuition as the payoff for having internalized everything before it. It transitions into the closing chapter on fear, which Hill treats as the primary obstacle preventing most readers from ever reaching this stage.
keyLessons: The sixth sense is presented as a capstone skill built on the other thirteen principles, not a starting point or shortcut.
The Invisible Counselors technique is best understood as a structured visualization exercise for decision-making, whatever metaphysical framing Hill gives it.
This is the most explicitly unfalsifiable chapter in the book and should be read as personal philosophy rather than a testable claim.

sections.title: How to Outwit the Six Ghosts of Fear
sections.summary: The closing chapter catalogues six basic fears — poverty, criticism, ill health, loss of love, old age, and death — and argues that most people are dominated by some combination of them without recognizing it, which quietly undermines every principle covered earlier. Hill provides a self-analysis questionnaire meant to expose which fears are active in the reader's own thinking, alongside worry, indecision, and doubt, which he treats as fear's close relatives. The chapter closes the book by returning to its opening claim: that thought, deliberately directed and freed from fear, is the one asset entirely within a person's control, and the entire preceding thirteen principles are tools for exercising that control.
keyLessons: Fear is treated as the master obstacle that undermines every other principle in the book if left unexamined.
The self-analysis questionnaire is offered as a diagnostic tool, not just a rhetorical device.
The book closes by returning full circle to its opening claim that controlled thought is the one truly controllable asset a person has.
Convert a vague wish into a burning desire by fixing an exact goal, a date, a plan, and a written statement you read aloud daily.
Treat indecision as a form of fear in disguise, and practice making decisions quickly while changing them slowly.
Build a genuine Mastermind alliance — people whose knowledge and effort complement your own, working in real harmony toward one aim.
Seek specialized knowledge organized around your specific goal rather than assuming general education or intelligence is enough.
Only emotionally charged thought, Hill argues, is acted on by the subconscious — repetition without feeling accomplishes little.
Audit yourself regularly against the thirty-one causes of failure and the six basic fears to catch what is quietly undermining your plan.
Persistence is a habit built through four concrete steps, not a personality trait you either have or lack.
Treat every idea as a recombination of existing elements — you don't need a wholly novel concept, just a useful new arrangement of known ones.

quotes.text: Whatever the mind can conceive and believe, it can achieve.
There is one quality which one must possess to win, and that is definiteness of purpose, the knowledge of what one wants, and a burning desire to possess it.
The starting point of all achievement is desire. Keep this constantly in mind. Weak desires bring weak results, just as a small fire makes a small amount of heat.
Faith is the head chemist of the mind. When faith is blended with the vibration of thought, the subconscious mind instantly picks up the vibration.
Truly, thoughts are things, and powerful things at that, when they are mixed with definiteness of purpose, persistence, and a burning desire for their translation into riches.
Persistence is to the character of man as carbon is to steel.

Before success comes in any man's life, he is sure to meet with much temporary defeat and, perhaps, some failure. When defeat overtakes a man, the easiest and most logical thing to do is to quit. That is exactly what the majority of men do.
Analysis of several hundred people who had accumulated fortunes well beyond the million-dollar mark disclosed the fact that every one of them had the habit of reaching decisions promptly.
There are two days in the week about which and upon which I never worry... Yesterday and Tomorrow.
Fears are nothing more than states of mind. One's state of mind is subject to control and direction.
No two minds ever come together without thereby creating a third, invisible, intangible force which may be likened to a third mind.

whoThisIsFor: Readers who want the foundational, original text behind the modern goal-setting and mindset genre, and who are comfortable separating its practical habits from its more metaphysical claims.
whenToReadThis: Useful at the start of a major personal or business goal, when you need a structured process for turning ambition into a written, dated plan rather than an open-ended wish.

authorBio.name: Napoleon Hill
authorBio.bio:
Napoleon Hill (1883–1970) was an American author and journalist from rural Virginia who built his career on the study of personal achievement, beginning with an assignment, by his own account, to interview Andrew Carnegie. That meeting led to a decades-long project interviewing prominent American businessmen and inventors, which Hill said formed the research basis for his philosophy of individual achievement.

Hill worked for a period as an advisor to President Franklin D. Roosevelt's administration and lectured widely on his success philosophy throughout his life. His reputation has always mixed genuine influence — Think and Grow Rich remains one of the best-selling books of the twentieth century — with unresolved questions about the accuracy of some of his biographical claims and business dealings, which biographers and journalists have scrutinized in the decades since his death.

He continued writing and revising his philosophy across several later books, cementing "success philosophy" as a durable, if contested, nonfiction genre that continues to shape self-help and business writing today.
notableWorks: Grow Rich! With Peace of Mind
Success Through a Positive Mental Attitude (with W. Clement Stone)

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Thirteen Steps to Riches
conceptsFrameworks.definition: The book's overall architecture: thirteen sequential principles (Desire, Faith, Autosuggestion, Specialized Knowledge, Imagination, Organized Planning, Decision, Persistence, Power of the Master Mind, Sex Transmutation, the Subconscious Mind, the Brain, and the Sixth Sense) that Hill claims, taken together, form a repeatable system for converting ambition into wealth.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: Structures the entire book, chapter by chapter.

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Master Mind
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Hill's term for the coordination of knowledge and effort between two or more people working in a spirit of genuine harmony toward a definite purpose, which he claims generates a third, more powerful collective intelligence beyond what either party possesses alone.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Sex Transmutation
conceptsFrameworks.definition: The claimed process of consciously redirecting sexual energy — which Hill treats as the most powerful human emotion — into creative, entrepreneurial, or artistic output rather than expressing it only physically.

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Six Ghosts of Fear
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Hill's taxonomy of the six basic fears — of poverty, criticism, ill health, loss of love, old age, and death — that he argues quietly dominate most people's thinking and undermine their pursuit of a definite chief aim.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: How to Outwit the Six Ghosts of Fear.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Definite Chief Aim
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A single, specific, written statement of exactly what a person wants, by when, and what they intend to give in return for it — the starting mechanism Hill says triggers every other principle in the book.

actionSteps: Write a one-paragraph definite chief aim statement specifying an exact goal, a target date, and what you're prepared to trade for it, then read it aloud morning and night for two weeks.
Identify one person whose specific knowledge or resources you lack and would need for your current goal, and reach out this week to propose a concrete, mutually beneficial way of working together.
Go through Hill's thirty-one causes of failure (or reconstruct a similar list from your own recurring setbacks) and honestly mark which three apply to you right now.
Practice one deliberate, time-boxed decision this week on something you've been putting off — set a hard deadline for the decision itself, separate from acting on it.
Take the six basic fears and write one sentence under each naming a specific way it currently shows up in your thinking, rather than treating fear as one undifferentiated feeling.
reflectionQuestions: Which of your current goals is still a wish rather than a burning desire, and what would it take to make it specific and dated?
Where in your life do you notice indecision quietly functioning as a socially acceptable form of fear?
Who in your circle actively reinforces your plans, and who quietly discourages them — and what would change if you spent more time with the former?
Which of the six basic fears do you suspect is doing the most damage to your ambitions right now, and why that one?

points: Many of the book's central claims about the causal power of thought are presented as established law but are not empirically testable in the form Hill states them, and modern readers should treat the "thoughts are things" framing as philosophy and motivational technique rather than demonstrated science.

The sex transmutation chapter rests on unverifiable claims about the private lives and motivations of historical figures, and its framing reflects 1930s assumptions about gender and sexuality that have not aged well.

The book's survivorship-bias structure — studying only people who became wealthy and inferring that their habits caused their wealth — does not rule out that timing, capital access, luck, and social position played a substantial role that the thirteen principles alone cannot replicate.
The Invisible Counselors and sixth-sense material is explicitly unfalsifiable, and Hill offers no way to distinguish genuine intuition from ordinary imagination within his own framework.

Some of the historical anecdotes used as evidence throughout the book (including several Edison and Ford stories) have been questioned or embellished in later biographical research, weakening their evidentiary value even as illustrative examples.
criticalTake.contextNote: Despite these limitations, the book's core behavioral prescriptions — specific written goals, deliberate persistence habits, and structured collaboration — anticipated much of the empirically grounded goal-setting research that emerged decades later, which is part of why the book has remained continuously influential rather than dated into irrelevance.

sourceNotes: This entry is based on general, well-established knowledge of Think and Grow Rich (1937), a widely documented and quoted classic; direct quotes are commonly reproduced across reputable literary sources and match well-known passages from the original English text. This entry describes the Vietnamese Yuan Phong translation's content only insofar as it follows the standard English edition — translator-specific wording or footnotes in that particular Vietnamese edition were not separately verified.
